overview: Dicraeosaurus (meaning 'forked lizard') was a medium-to-large sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Jurassic period, approximately 161–143 million years ago, in what is now Tanzania and possibly Zimbabwe. Estimated at up to 20 metres in length, it was a member of Dicraeosauridae, a family of diplodocoid sauropods characterised by bifurcated (forked) neural spines that formed a prominent ridge along the neck and back. Its fossils come primarily from the world-famous Tendaguru Formation.

Dicraeosaurus was described by Werner Janensch in 1914 following large-scale German excavations at Tendaguru in the early twentieth century. As one of the best-known dicraeosaurids, it provides important evidence for understanding the diversity of diplodocoid sauropods on Gondwana. The forked neural spines may have supported a fleshy dorsal crest or served as muscle attachment sites, though the exact function remains debated.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Dicraeosaurus was named by Werner Janensch in 1914 from specimens collected during the Tendaguru expeditions (1909–1913), one of the most ambitious fossil-collecting efforts of the early twentieth century. The type species, D. hansemanni, honours Consul-General Hans Meyer and reflects the diplomatic context of colonial-era German palaeontology in East Africa.

articles.title: The Forked Spines
articles.body: The genus name references the distinctive bifurcated neural spines crowning the vertebrae of the neck and trunk, which gave Dicraeosaurus a sail-like or ridged profile. Similar structures appear in the closely related Amargasaurus from South America. The spines may have functioned in display, thermoregulation, or as anchor points for enlarged neck muscles.

articles.title: Phylogenetic Position
articles.body: Dicraeosauridae is a well-supported family within Diplodocoidea, sharing with diplodocids a peglike dentition, elongated neck, and whip-like tail. Dicraeosaurids are generally shorter-necked and smaller-bodied than classic diplodocids, suggesting a different niche, possibly browsing at lower vegetation heights.

articles.title: Tendaguru Ecosystem
articles.body: Dicraeosaurus shared the Tendaguru landscape with Brachiosaurus, Giraffatitan, and several stegosaurs, constituting a diverse Late Jurassic fauna comparable to the Morrison Formation of North America. This parallel diversity has informed biogeographical hypotheses about faunal exchange between northern and southern landmasses during the Jurassic.

record.description: Dicraeosaurus hansemanni was a short-necked, quadrupedal herbivorous dicraeosaurid from the Lower and Middle Dinosaur members of the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania. Several partial skeletons and skull material make it comparatively informative, but the material is disarticulated and distributed among individuals.
facts: D. hansemanni occurs lower in the Tendaguru succession than D. sattleri and the two species should not be conflated.
Skulls, vertebral columns and limb elements document a relatively short neck and bifid neural spines.
The old 150-135 Ma range is too young and too broad for the type species.

review.ageReviewNote: Corrected from an erroneous Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous range to the Kimmeridgian lower/middle Tendaguru record.
